opus-5.5.text:
Well, the starting point is that the classical definition of rationality, the one that runs through economics, decision theory, and a lot of early AI, says a rational agent picks the action that maximizes expected utility given what it knows. That's a beautiful definition, but it's not achievable. For any interesting environment, like chess, let alone the real world, computing the truly optimal action is wildly intractable. So if you say "build a perfectly rational agent," you've given the engineer a specification that no physical machine can meet. That's not very helpful.

There were various responses to this. Herb Simon talked about bounded rationality and satisficing, which was an important insight, but it was more descriptive than prescriptive. It didn't tell you what you *should* build. And in AI there was a lot of work on metareasoning: how much should the system think before it acts, which computations are worth doing.

What Devika Subramanian and I tried to do in the early nineties was flip the question. Instead of asking for the optimal *action*, which you can't compute, ask for the optimal *program*. Fix the machine architecture you actually have, with its memory and speed, fix the class of environments the agent will operate in, and fix a performance measure. Then a boundedly optimal agent is the program that, running on that machine, does at least as well as any other program on that machine would do in those environments. That's a well-defined target. It exists, at least in principle, because you're optimizing over a set of programs that can actually run.

The appeal is that it reframes AI as an engineering discipline with a real objective. It also tells you that the right design might look nothing like "think hard and pick the best action." It might involve reflexes, caching, compiled heuristics, anytime algorithms that you interrupt when time runs out, because deliberation itself costs something. A human expert doesn't recompute everything from first principles; they've compiled a lot of experience into fast responses, and bounded optimality explains why that's rational rather than a defect.

Now, the honest caveat is that finding the boundedly optimal program is itself usually intractable. We were able to prove results for fairly restricted settings, for example with certain classes of anytime algorithms and time-dependent utility, where you can show a particular scheduling of computations is optimal or asymptotically so. For general intelligence we don't have a recipe. But I think it's still the right way to think about what we're aiming for, and in some sense learning, including the large-scale learning we see today, can be viewed as a search through program space for something approximately boundedly optimal for the training distribution.

And I'd add one more thing that's become central to how I think now. All of this assumes the performance measure is given and correct. Bounded optimality tells you how to do well with respect to an objective under computational limits. It says nothing about whether the objective is the right one. And that, I've come to believe, is the bigger problem: we've built the whole field around optimizing fixed objectives that we specify, and we don't actually know how to specify them correctly. So the next step is to combine both kinds of humility: the machine is limited in what it can compute, and it's uncertain about what humans actually want.

r001.rationale: Defines a boundedly optimal agent as a program that performs at least as well as any other program executable on the fixed machine, for the specified environments and performance measure.

r002.rationale: Explicitly shifts the target from choosing an optimal action to choosing an optimal program, explaining that the action-level target is computationally infeasible.

r003.rationale: Does not explain that changing a locally suboptimal action could worsen the program’s overall performance.

r004.rationale: Does not describe composing boundedly optimal components by chaining their simpler objectives.

r005.rationale: Says fixed objectives may be incorrectly specified and presents uncertainty about human preferences as the next step, communicating that building agents around fixed objectives is inadequate.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, bounded optimality came out of a frustration I had early on, which is that the standard definitions of intelligence we had inherited from economics and philosophy were, strictly speaking, definitions of something that can't exist. The classical notion is perfect rationality: an agent that always takes the action maximizing expected utility given its beliefs. That's a beautiful mathematical object, but no physical system can be perfectly rational, because computing the optimal action in any realistic situation takes astronomically more time than you have. By the time you've finished deciding the perfect move, the game is over, the tiger has eaten you, and so on.

So there was a period where people, including Herb Simon, said, fine, let's talk about bounded rationality instead, let's talk about satisficing, about agents that do "well enough." But that was never really a definition. It described a phenomenon rather than specifying what you should build. And then there were attempts in the eighties, including some of my own work with Eric Wefald, on what you might call calculative rationality or metareasoning, where the agent deliberates about how long to deliberate. That's useful, but it has a recursion problem. If you have to compute the value of computation, and that computation itself takes time, you're off into an infinite regress unless you cut it off somewhere, and the cutoff is arbitrary.

Bounded optimality tries to get out of this by shifting what we're optimizing over. Instead of asking "what is the optimal action?", which the agent can't compute, we ask "what is the optimal program?" You fix the machine. It has a certain processor, a certain amount of memory, a certain speed. You fix the environment class the agent will operate in. And then the bounded optimal agent is the program, among all the programs that can actually run on that machine, that produces the best expected outcome in that environment. The optimization is done by the designer, in a sense offline, not by the agent at run time.

What I like about this is that it's a real definition. It's well-defined, the object exists, and it's the right thing to aspire to. It also makes rationality a property of the design rather than a property of each individual decision, which I think matches how we actually judge intelligent systems and, frankly, people. We don't say someone is irrational because they didn't compute the globally optimal choice at the supermarket; we say they're sensible if their overall policy for getting through life works out well given the brain they've got.

Now, there are complications. For most interesting machines and environments, you can't literally find the bounded optimal program either, because the space of programs is enormous. So in the original paper with Devika Subramanian we introduced the idea of asymptotic bounded optimality, roughly borrowing the move computer science makes with complexity theory: your program is asymptotically bounded optimal if, given a machine that's a constant factor faster, it does at least as well as any program on the original machine. That gets you something achievable and lets you prove results about real algorithm construction, like how to compose anytime algorithms into a bounded optimal whole.

I'd say the framework has been more influential as a conceptual stance than as a toolkit people use daily. It tells you that the right unit of analysis for AI is the agent program in its environment, under its computational constraints, and that questions like "how much should I think before acting" are first-class design questions, not afterthoughts. And I think that stance is even more relevant now. Large models, for instance, are a case where someone chose, more or less implicitly, how to spend a fixed computational budget, and the interesting questions about test-time compute and reasoning length are exactly bounded optimality questions, even if nobody calls them that.

r001.rationale: It defines the bounded optimal agent as the executable program that produces the best expected outcome among programs that can run on a fixed machine in a fixed environment.

r002.rationale: It says optimization is a design task over the agent program, shifting rationality from individual decisions to the overall policy.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes program-level rationality from individual decisions but does not say that correcting a locally suboptimal action would worsen the program’s overall performance.

r004.rationale: It mentions composing anytime algorithms into a bounded optimal whole, but does not describe composing bounded optimal components by chaining their simpler objectives.

r005.rationale: It does not express a revised judgment that building agents with fixed objectives is the wrong approach.

astra-6.text:
Well, bounded optimality starts with the observation that an agent has to make decisions using a physical machine, and that machine has finite computational resources. So asking it to always choose the best possible action, regardless of how much computation that requires, isn’t a very useful prescription.

Instead, we ask: what is the best program that could run on this machine? Given its memory, its speed, and the kinds of environments it will encounter, which program produces the best expected performance? That shifts the object of optimization from individual actions to the agent’s program as a whole.

For example, a program that calculates a perfect decision but finishes after the deadline may be worse than one that produces a reasonably good decision quickly. The cost of deliberation is part of the problem, because the world continues to change while you’re thinking.

I see this as a useful foundation for AI because it makes computational limitations intrinsic to the theory. It doesn’t immediately tell us how to build the best agent—that can still be an extraordinarily difficult problem—but it gives us a coherent target: the best achievable behavior given the resources available.

r001.rationale: It defines the target as the best-performing program that can run on a machine with finite resources, given its expected environments.

r002.rationale: It says optimization shifts from individual actions to the agent’s program, but does not explain that designers control programs rather than individual actions.

r003.rationale: It does not explain how correcting a locally suboptimal action could worsen the program’s overall performance.

r004.rationale: It does not describe composing a system from bounded optimal components or chaining their objectives.

r005.rationale: It does not state that Russell revised his view and considers fixed-objective AI agents the wrong approach.

sol-6.1.text:
Bounded optimality starts from the observation that an agent is a physical system with finite computational resources. So it makes little sense to define intelligence as always choosing the best possible action, if figuring out that action requires more computation than the agent could ever perform.

Instead, we ask: what is the best program that could run on a particular machine, given the environments in which it has to operate? That shifts the object of optimization from individual actions to the program that generates behavior. The program has to manage its computational limitations, including deciding how much time to spend thinking before acting.

For example, a chess program that finds a brilliant move after the clock has expired isn't doing a good job. We want a program whose overall behavior makes the best use of the resources available to it.

I see this as a more coherent foundation for AI than taking perfect rationality as the definition and then apologizing whenever we approximate it. The resource constraints are part of the problem from the outset. Of course, that doesn't make finding the optimal program easy, but it gives us a clearer account of what we're trying to achieve.

r001.rationale: It asks for the best program that can run on a particular machine across its environments, and describes optimizing the program’s overall behavior under its resource limits.

r002.rationale: It explicitly shifts optimization from individual actions to the program that generates behavior.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that correcting a locally suboptimal action could worsen the program’s overall performance.

r004.rationale: It does not describe composing bounded optimal systems from components or chaining their objectives.

r005.rationale: It favors bounded optimality over perfect rationality, but does not say that building agents with fixed objectives is the wrong approach.
